extracted.intended_audience: Companies and stakeholders operating in Europe concerned with patent protection and enforcement (patent owners, licensees, implementers, in-house counsel and external patent litigators)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting, obtaining and litigating European patents under the Unitary Patent Package (Unitary Patent and Unified Patent Court), including timing, filing, opt-out/opt-in choices, venue/litigation tactics, costs, and portfolio-level decisions. Focused on practical strategy for patentees, implementers and licensees in participating EU Member States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting unitary effect: timing, fee and translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the EPO has decided that a European patent application can proceed to grant, the patentee then has one month from the date of grant to request that the patent should be given unitary effect. No fee is payable and only one translation will be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request must be made within one month of the date of publication of the grant in the European Patent Bulletin. For a transitional period (at least 6 years) an additional translation will be required: into English if the patent language is French or German; into any other official EU language if the patent language is English. No fee to request unitary effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unitary Patent renewal fees and 'all-or-nothing' character
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a single renewal fee instead of a renewal fee per country; set to be equivalent to renewal fees for a European patent validated in the top four states (UK not part of UPP). The Unitary Patent cannot be 'pruned'—patentee cannot drop countries over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The single renewal fee was calculated to be roughly equivalent to renewals in Germany, France, The Netherlands and (previously) the UK; over 20 years the example sum is ca. €35,500 if granted in the year of application. Financial disadvantage: inability to drop individual countries—Unitary Patent is 'all or nothing'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive UPC jurisdiction and its consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Unitary Patents are subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the UPC. An injunction granted by a single court will stop infringements in all participating Member States. Conversely, a Unitary Patent remains vulnerable throughout its life to being revoked in an action before a single court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single decision can grant or wipe out patent protection across the entire UPC zone; patentees must weigh broad, fast relief against centralised revocation risk ('all the patent eggs in one basket'). Consider litigation and enforcement trade‑offs when choosing unitary effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three options for obtaining patent protection in Europe
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees have three routes: (1) Traditional European patent validated in chosen EPC contracting states (no unitary effect); (2) European patent with unitary effect (Unitary Patent) requested within one month of grant; (3) National patents via national patent offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each option has pros/cons: national patents can be quicker/cheaper for limited jurisdictions; Unitary Patent offers broad coverage and single renewal but central revocation risk; traditional European patents with targeted validations permit selective national protection and opt-outs to avoid UPC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unitary Patent not available for opt-out; opt-out limited to European patents/applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Opt-outs are only available for European patents and patent applications (not Unitary Patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees who wish to exclude a patent from UPC jurisdiction must use opt-out on European patents/applications before the UPC has competence for that patent; Unitary Patents are automatically subject to UPC jurisdiction and cannot be opted out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opt-out availability, requirements and effects (Art. 83)
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners/applicants of European patents granted or applied for prior to the end of the transitional period may opt out from the exclusive competence of the Court. The opt-out shall take effect upon its entry into the register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opt-out cannot be filed if an action has already been brought before the Court. Opt-out must be filed on behalf of all actual patent owners for all EPC Member States where the patent is validated (not just UPC Member States). There is no fee. Opt-out remains effective (unless withdrawn) for the life of the patent and any subsequent SPCs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal of opt-out (opting back in) and blocking events
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees who opted out may withdraw their opt-out (opt back in) at any time provided no national proceedings have previously been commenced (post 1 June 2023) in relation to the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawal takes effect upon entry in the register. National proceedings started after 1 June 2023 will prevent withdrawal; national proceedings filed before 1 June 2023 do not block withdrawal (confirmed by UPC Court of Appeal). There is no fee to withdraw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional period jurisdictional scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC will have non-exclusive jurisdiction over all existing European patents validated in participating Member States during the 'transitional period' of 7 years (possibly extendable by a further 7 years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During transition, patentees must manage the interplay between national courts and the UPC; opt-outs can be filed until one month before the end of the transitional period. Consider timing of actions and opt-outs while transitional rules apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue and forum selection rules for infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may bring an infringement action either in the local or regional division where infringement occurs or in a jurisdiction where the defendant resides or has a place of business. For non-participating EU Member State defendants, a patentee may also bring an infringement action at the central division. A defendant cannot transfer an infringement action from a local division to the central division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose venue with attention to local/regional/central division subject-matter allocations, languages, and 'couleur locale'. Forum shopping risks and advantages require careful consideration when deciding where to start proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central division exclusive jurisdiction and case allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: The central division has exclusive jurisdiction over declarations of non-infringement and revocation actions (other than counterclaims). If a revocation action is pending at the central division, the patentee may bring an infringement action in the central division too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a counterclaim for revocation arises, local/regional divisions have options: keep the case, refer the counterclaim to the central division and keep or stay infringement, or refer the entire case to the central division (with parties' agreement). Allocation rules affect strategy for combining or separating invalidity and infringement proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bifurcation, stays and 'high likelihood' invalidity threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Bifurcation is procedurally possible. In the event of bifurcation, an infringement action will be stayed where there is a 'high likelihood' of the relevant claims being held invalid (UPC Rules of Procedure Rules 37.4 and 118.2(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice bifurcation has been rare and tends to occur where another revocation action is already pending. Where the counterclaim is referred to the central division but there is no stay, the judge rapporteur will endeavour to set the revocation hearing before the infringement hearing (Rule 40(b)). Tactical timing of revocation/infringement filings matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: UPC structure, seats and subject-matter allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC Court of First Instance has a Central Division (Paris, Munich, Milan with seats and subject-matter specialities), Local Divisions (in participating states) and a Court of Appeal in Luxembourg. Subject-matter specialisations: Paris (electronics, SPCs), Munich (mechanical engineering, chemistry excluding SPCs), Milan (human necessities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local/regional divisions handle infringement and counterclaims for revocation. Regional divisions (e.g., Nordic-Baltic) exist. Differences in local practice ('couleur locale') may influence choice of division and case preparation. Training centres and PMAC (mediation) are also being established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of proceedings and 'English limited rule'
rubrics_metrics.description: Language of the proceedings is the language in which the patent was granted (English, French or German). English is available in all divisions. Local divisions may allow pleadings in the local language if the language of litigation is English, but reserve the right to hold oral hearings and issue judgments in the local language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice English is generally used when English is the language of litigation; however, local variations exist and parties should plan for possible local-language requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: UPC procedural features: speed, discovery, evidence and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings on the merits are expected to be concluded in slightly over 1 year. Applications for preliminary measures (including preliminary injunctions) can be available rapidly. The UPC offers no or only limited documentary discovery and non-oral discovery and no or very limited oral testimony, resulting in shorter trials. Seizure of evidence is possible in some circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features make UPC proceedings generally faster and, in many cases, cheaper than US district court litigation. Parties should prepare concise documentary evidence and anticipate limited oral testimony; early preservation and seizure options can be relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs, fees and recoverable costs in UPC proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic infringement actions cost €11,000 plus a sliding scale value-based fee (€0 - 325,000). Revocation actions cost €20,000 (fixed fee). Application for provisional measures cost €11,000 (fixed fee). Micro and small enterprises are entitled to a 40% reduction on all court fees incurred in the Court of First Instance and Court of Appeal. The scale of recoverable costs ranges from €38,000 to €2,000,000 depending on value of proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No fee to opt-out or to withdraw an opt-out. Losing party will in most cases be expected to pay a significant proportion of the winning party’s costs. Budgeting for both fixed and value-based fees and considering SME reductions is important for strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolio-level strategy: choosing patent types and combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees should develop a tailored patent filing and litigation strategy considering a mix of European patents, Unitary Patents and national patents. Options include: same type for all inventions (simple), using national patents where protection only needed in a few jurisdictions, Unitary Patents for strong patents requiring pan‑Europe protection, traditional European patents with opt-outs for economically important but less-certain patents, and combinations such as parent unitaries with opted‑out divisionals having wider scope (subject to EPC double patenting prohibition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider cost-effectiveness, geographical coverage, strength of patent, enforcement requirements, and interplay with opt-outs and divisionals. Use divisional strategy to balance central enforcement risk and national fallback positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee and implemeter considerations and tactical measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensees should check licence terms for opt-out/ enforcement rights: exclusive licensees may enforce a patent without patentee consent (unless licence states otherwise); non-exclusive licensees typically cannot. Implementers should consider early validity attack strategies and protective measures such as filing a 'Protective Letter' with the UPC to reduce the risk of ex‑parte preliminary measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementers can start central revocation actions against non‑opted patents but should expect patentee responses (central infringement actions). For opted‑out patents, starting national revocation proceedings prevents opt‑in and keeps litigation national. Monitor European Patent Register for opt‑out status and set alerts.
